title: Camera obscura
wiki_lead:
A camera obscura (pl. camerae obscurae or camera obscuras; from Latin  camera obscūra 'dark chamber') is the natural phenomenon in which light passing through the small hole of a dark chamber or box will project an image of a scene outside the chamber (box) onto the surface opposite to the hole, resulting in an inverted (upside down) and reversed (left to right) projection of the view outside.
Camera obscura refers to analogous constructions such as a darkened room, box or tent in which an exterior image is projected inside or onto a translucent screen viewed from outside. Camera obscuras with a lens in the opening have been used since the second half of the 16th century and became popular as aids for drawing and painting. The technology was developed further into the photographic camera in the first half of the 19th century, when camera obscura boxes were used to expose light-sensitive materials to the projected image.
The image (or the principle of its projection) of a lensless camera obscura is also referred to as a "pinhole image".
The camera obscura was used to study eclipses without the risk of damaging the eyes by looking directly into the Sun. As a drawing aid, it allowed tracing the projected image to produce a highly accurate representation, and was especially appreciated as an easy way to achieve proper graphical perspective.
Before the term camera obscura was first used in 1604, other terms were used to refer to the devices: cubiculum obscurum, cubiculum tenebricosum, conclave obscurum, and locus obscurus.
A camera obscura without a lens but with a very small hole is sometimes referred to as a "pinhole camera", although this more often refers to simple (homemade) lensless cameras where photographic film or photographic paper is used.

Physical explanation
Rays of light travel in straight lines and change when they are reflected and partly absorbed by an object, retaining information about the color and brightness of the surface of that object. Lighted objects reflect rays of light in all directions. A small enough opening in a barrier admits only the rays that travel directly from different points in the scene on the other side, and these rays form an image of that scene where they reach a surface opposite from the opening.
The human eye (and that of many other animals) works much like a camera obscura, with rays of light entering an opening (pupil), getting focused through a convex lens and passing a dark chamber before forming an inverted image on a smooth surface (retina). The analogy appeared early in the 16th century and would in the 17th century find common use to illustrate Western theological ideas about God creating the universe as a machine, with a predetermined purpose (just like humans create machines). This had a huge influence on behavioral science, especially on the study of perception and cognition. grok_lead: The camera obscura, from the Latin words meaning "dark chamber," is a simple optical device that projects an inverted and reversed image of its surroundings onto a surface inside a darkened enclosure through a small aperture or lens, demonstrating the basic principles of image formation via light rays. The concept dates back to ancient times, with the earliest recorded description by the Chinese philosopher Mozi (c. 470â391 BCE), who observed that light passing through a small hole in a dark room produces an inverted image on the opposite wall. Around 350 BCE, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described a similar effect while studying solar eclipses, noting how light projected through gaps in leaves formed crescent-shaped images on the ground, which he used to safely observe the phenomenon without direct eye exposure. In the 11th century, the Arab physicist and mathematician Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham, 965â1040 CE) provided the first comprehensive scientific analysis in his Book of Optics, explaining the pinhole projection mechanism and applying it to eclipse observation and vision studies. During the Renaissance, the device evolved with the addition of convex lenses to sharpen and brighten images, first suggested by Italian scholar Girolamo Cardano in 1550 and further detailed by Giovanni Battista della Porta in 1558, who incorporated mirrors for upright projections. The term camera obscura was coined by German astronomer Johannes Kepler in the early 17th century, building on these advancements to refine its use in optics research. Portable versions, such as lidded boxes or tents, became popular among artists and travelers by the 16th century, enabling precise sketching of landscapes and architecture during the Grand Tour era. The camera obscura served multiple purposes across history, including as a safe tool for astronomers like John Flamsteed in 1684 to view sunspots and eclipses, and as an aid for painters such as Leonardo da Vinci (1452â1519), who recommended it for achieving accurate perspective in drawings, and Johannes Vermeer (1632â1675), whose works show evidence of optical projection techniques. In the 19th century, it transitioned into entertainment at seaside resorts, like the 1829 Clifton Observatory in England, and military applications for reconnaissance during World War II. Ultimately, it laid the groundwork for photography, with Joseph NiÃ©pce capturing the first permanent image using a camera obscura in 1826â1827, marking the shift from transient projections to fixed records.
